paragraphs: CoMLSim addresses the problem of using machine learning to simulate steady-state partial differential equations on finely resolved grids. Its central idea is to combine principles from traditional numerical solvers with learning that operates locally. The method also uses low-dimensional representations and repeated inference steps to build simulations across large computational domains.

This combination matters because the paper targets generalization across more than the conditions represented during training. The evaluated changes include unfamiliar source terms, geometries, and domain sizes. Local learning and iterative simulation provide the organizing approach for handling these changes, rather than treating each large simulation as an entirely separate prediction problem.

The authors validate CoMLSim on more than five steady-state PDEs under different conditions, comparing it with Ansys Fluent and four machine-learning methods. Their numerical experiments show better accuracy and generalization than the machine-learning baselines. Component-removal experiments also identify parts of the approach that strongly affect results. These findings support the authors’ conclusion that local learning and iterative inference reduce generalization difficulties in the settings tested; they do not establish superiority over the commercial solver.
neurips-2022-a-composable-machine-learni.tldr: CoMLSim combines local learning with iterative PDE simulation to improve accuracy and generalization over tested machine-learning baselines.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms update several quantities that depend on one another while using noisy information. This paper studies how quickly such coupled stochastic approximation procedures converge when their updates operate on a single timescale. The aim is to identify settings where carefully analyzing these interactions yields stronger guarantees without relying on separate update timescales.

The analysis centers on smoothness of the fixed points associated with the coupled sequences. Informally, this concerns how regularly their equilibrium values change as related quantities change. Under this property and strongly monotone increments for every sequence, the authors establish an iteration requirement of order one over the target accuracy. This improves an existing dependence of order accuracy to the power minus one-and-a-half for two coupled sequences.

When the main sequence lacks a strongly monotone increment, the stated iteration requirement becomes order one over accuracy squared. The distinction makes the assumptions consequential: the faster guarantee does not apply indiscriminately. Applications to stochastic bilevel optimization, compositional optimization, and reinforcement learning recover the best known guarantees or improve existing ones, demonstrating the usefulness of a shared analysis across several learning problems.
neurips-2022-a-single-timescale-analysis.tldr: A single-timescale analysis gives sharper conditional convergence guarantees for stochastic algorithms with multiple interacting update sequences.

paragraphs: Offline model-based reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to learn how an environment changes, then uses that model and the fixed data to learn a policy. No further interaction with the environment is available. The paper examines a mismatch in many existing approaches: the objective used to train the environment model is separate from the objective used to improve the policy.

That separation can matter because improving a model according to its own training objective may not translate into better decisions. The proposed framework connects the two learning processes through a lower bound on the policy’s true expected return. It alternates between updating the dynamics model and updating the policy while pursuing this common objective.

The contribution is therefore a unified way to organize offline learning, with model training and policy improvement explicitly linked. Experiments on a broad range of continuous-control offline datasets show competitive performance. This supports the practical value of addressing objective mismatch, while the stated result remains competitive performance rather than a claim that the framework universally surpasses other offline reinforcement-learning methods.
neurips-2022-a-unified-framework-for-alt.tldr: The framework alternates dynamics-model training and policy learning around a shared lower bound on expected return.

paragraphs: A differential equation can describe a system whose external driving input is unknown. This paper asks how noisy measurements of the system can reveal that input, called the forcing function, together with other unknown parameters. It represents the forcing with a Gaussian process, allowing inference about an unknown function rather than only a small set of numbers.

The method combines the adjoint of a linear system with a finite basis approximation of the Gaussian-process kernel. This creates a setting where conjugate Bayesian inference can be performed exactly for the truncated representation. The qualification matters: inference is exact within that finite approximation, while the original Gaussian process has been approximated. In many cases, this requires substantially less computation than MCMC.

Demonstrations cover both ordinary and partial differential equations. The authors find that a modest number of basis vectors can approximate the true forcing well in these examples. They also use Bayesian optimization to obtain point estimates of nonlinear parameters, including kernel length-scales. Together, these steps provide an efficient route to recovering hidden inputs while handling different kinds of unknowns through distinct inference procedures.
neurips-2022-adjoint-aided-inference-of-.tldr: Adjoint calculations enable efficient Bayesian inference of unknown forcing functions represented by truncated Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a local criterion for evaluating electoral district plans. A complaint arises when a contiguous, population-balanced region contains a majority sharing an interest whose members are minorities in their assigned districts. Such a region is called a deviating group. A plan is locally fair when no group meeting this definition exists.

This criterion examines how district boundaries divide geographically connected populations with shared interests. The authors prove that auditing a plan for local fairness is NP-complete, establishing a computational obstacle to checking the condition in general. They develop an MCMC approach for auditing and ranking plans, alongside a dynamic-programming auditing algorithm used to assess the MCMC method’s effectiveness.

Tests using real election data find plans that are exactly or nearly locally fair. The authors also show that such plans can be produced with little sacrifice in compactness, district competitiveness, or plan-level seat shares in the examined settings. The findings make local fairness a practical additional perspective for evaluating redistricting, with evidence that it can coexist with established criteria rather than necessarily demanding large tradeoffs.
neurips-2022-all-politics-is-local-redis.tldr: The paper defines local fairness for redistricting and develops methods that find nearly or exactly fair plans in real election data.

paragraphs: Understanding animal movement in video requires both locating body keypoints and tracking animals across frames. The paper identifies a dataset gap: earlier animal datasets focused on tracking or pose estimation in individual images, without supporting both together. APT-36K supplies a benchmark designed to evaluate these connected parts of video-based animal analysis.

The dataset contains 2,400 video clips covering 30 animal species. Each clip contributes 15 frames, producing 36,000 frames overall. All animal instances receive manually created keypoint and tracking annotations, which are double-checked. This provides linked information about body configuration and animal identity across the selected video frames.

The authors benchmark representative models in three settings: single-frame pose estimation with transfer learning, generalization to unseen animal species, and pose estimation combined with tracking. These settings distinguish learning within familiar conditions from transferring knowledge to different domains or animals. The experiments support the dataset’s usefulness as a research benchmark and expose challenges for future methods. Its contribution is shared evaluation infrastructure for capabilities relevant to applications such as understanding animal behavior in wildlife conservation.
neurips-2022-apt-36k-a-large-scale-bench.tldr: APT-36K provides 36,000 annotated video frames for jointly studying animal pose estimation, tracking, and transfer across species.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision problems with a finite horizon and unknown parameters, such as transition probabilities estimated from data. Planning must therefore account for uncertainty about the model itself. The authors note that distributionally robust approaches can sometimes respond too conservatively, motivating a formulation that permits more flexible attitudes toward parameter uncertainty.

Their Bayesian risk Markov decision process represents unknown parameters through Bayesian posterior distributions. A risk functional is applied in a nested way to expected total cost, incorporating how uncertainty is treated across decision stages. The formulation also accounts for data becoming available at future stages, connecting current decisions with the prospect of learning more about the environment.

For the conditional value-at-risk risk functional, the authors develop an efficient approximation algorithm. It combines an analytical approximation of the value function with the convexity of CVaR. Experiments on a gambler’s betting problem and an inventory-control problem demonstrate the formulation and algorithms empirically. The contribution is a framework for risk-sensitive planning under parameter uncertainty, together with a computational approach for a particular risk choice.
neurips-2022-bayesian-risk-markov-decisi.tldr: Bayesian risk MDPs combine posterior uncertainty, flexible risk preferences, and future data availability in finite-horizon planning.

paragraphs: Learning in recurrent networks requires assigning credit to earlier interactions that influenced later outcomes. Backpropagation through time performs this role in artificial networks, but implementing its signaling requirements in biological networks is difficult. This paper proposes that locally diffusing neuromodulators, such as neuropeptides, could provide a biologically plausible way to carry temporal credit information.

The proposed update rule, ModProp, approximates gradient-based learning while allowing credit to propagate across arbitrary numbers of time steps. It goes beyond approximations that explicitly truncate the temporal span. Its mechanism combines modulatory signals with receiving cells’ eligibility traces through causal filters whose behavior is time-invariant and specific to synapse type.

Mathematical analysis and simulations on benchmark temporal tasks show advantages over existing biologically plausible temporal credit-assignment rules. These results support a possible mechanism for communicating the consequences of recurrent interactions over longer horizons; they do not establish that biological networks actually implement it. The authors also derive a computational implementation that could offer a causal, low-complexity alternative to backpropagation through time, connecting the biological proposal to an artificial learning algorithm.
neurips-2022-biologically-plausible-back.tldr: ModProp proposes local neuromodulator signaling as a biologically plausible mechanism for approximate credit assignment across long temporal spans.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves a learning problem whose objective depends on another optimization problem. It appears in tasks including hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, continual learning, and reinforcement learning. The paper addresses the computational difficulty of connecting these two levels, particularly when the underlying functions are large and non-convex, as in deep learning.

Conventional approaches use implicit differentiation and calculations involving the Hessian matrix to account for the lower-level optimization. BOME instead relies only on first-order gradients. The authors present it as a simple, practical algorithm that avoids implicit differentiation, addressing both computational expense and the complexity of earlier attempts to make bilevel methods depend only on first-order information.

The paper provides a non-asymptotic convergence analysis, meaning that its guarantees concern finite computational progress rather than only eventual behavior. Those guarantees target stationary points for non-convex objectives, not globally optimal solutions. Empirical results show superior practical performance in the reported comparisons. Together, the analysis and experiments support the claim that a simpler gradient-only approach can make bilevel optimization practical for large-scale deep-learning problems.
neurips-2022-bome-bilevel-optimization-m.tldr: BOME uses only first-order gradients for bilevel optimization, with finite-time stationary-point guarantees and strong reported practical performance.

paragraphs: Generating text does not require the same amount of computation for every prediction. Some continuations benefit from a language model’s full capacity, while others are easier. Confident Adaptive Language Modeling, or CALM, uses this variation to allocate computation dynamically for each input and each generation step, allowing sufficiently confident predictions to exit early.

Making early exits work requires more than choosing a stopping threshold. The framework addresses how to measure confidence and how to relate individual token decisions to requirements on the complete generated sequence. It also handles a dependency created by previous exits: later tokens may need to attend to hidden representations that were never computed for earlier tokens.

The authors combine theoretical analysis with experiments on three different text-generation tasks. They demonstrate reduced computation, with potential speedups of up to three times, while providing guarantees for maintaining high performance. The word potential matters here: the stated speedup concerns the opportunity offered by reduced computation. The contribution is an approach that connects local computational savings with sequence-level quality, while accounting for dependencies between successive generation steps.
neurips-2022-confident-adaptive-language.tldr: CALM adapts computation at each generation step, offering potential speedups of up to three times with performance guarantees.

paragraphs: DataMUX explores whether a neural network can make separate predictions for several inputs after processing them together in one compact representation. Each input first undergoes a fixed linear transformation. The transformed inputs are combined into a mixture with the same size as one input, allowing the base network to process shared representational space.

A demultiplexing layer then turns the network’s output into separate representations for individual predictions. The objective is higher inference throughput with little additional memory. The paper evaluates six tasks spanning sentence classification, named entity recognition, and image classification. Its evidence is strongest for Transformers, with viability demonstrated to a much smaller extent for MLPs and CNNs.

On MNLI, multiplexing up to 20 or 40 inputs yields throughput increases of up to 11 or 18 times, respectively, compared with a standard Transformer. The corresponding absolute performance drops are below two and four percentage points. These results show a measured throughput–accuracy tradeoff rather than cost-free acceleration. The paper also supplies a theoretical construction for self-attention multiplexing and examines how design choices affect the approach.
neurips-2022-datamux-data-multiplexing-f.tldr: DataMUX mixes multiple inputs into one compact network representation to increase inference throughput with measured accuracy tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Distributed learning often spends substantial effort communicating gradients between workers. Compression reduces the information sent, but introduces errors that optimization algorithms must handle. The paper connects two previously separate approaches: variance reduction for unbiased random compression, represented by DIANA, and error feedback for biased contractive compression, represented by EF21.

The proposed framework describes compression through two parameters, bias and variance, covering a larger class of operators. Its algorithm includes DIANA and EF21 as special cases. This common formulation allows biased compression, such as top-k, while also exploiting independent randomness across workers to reduce the impact of compression on convergence.

That combination matters because increasing the number of parallel workers can improve the convergence rate while retaining access to practically useful biased compressors. The authors prove linear convergence under specified conditions, so this rate is a conditional theoretical result. The contribution is both an algorithm and a unified explanation of how error feedback and variance reduction can work together, replacing separate analyses with a framework that captures benefits from each.
neurips-2022-ef-bv-a-unified-theory-of-e.tldr: EF-BV unifies error feedback and variance reduction to support biased compression and benefit from independent randomness across workers.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how autoregressive Transformer language models store and retrieve factual associations. The authors develop causal interventions that identify activations decisive for factual predictions. Their analysis points to particular computations in middle-layer feed-forward modules while the model processes subject tokens, providing evidence that some factual associations involve localized, editable mechanisms.

To test that interpretation, the authors introduce Rank-One Model Editing, or ROME. It changes feed-forward weights to update particular factual associations. This connects a proposed explanation of factual recall to a concrete intervention: if the identified computations matter, modifying them should change the corresponding factual predictions in useful and targeted ways.

ROME performs comparably to existing methods on the standard zsRE editing task. On a new counterfactual-assertion dataset, it preserves both specificity and generalization, whereas compared methods trade off one against the other. These properties concern keeping edits targeted while allowing them to carry across relevant expressions. The findings support an important role for middle-layer feed-forward modules and suggest that directly modifying identified computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach to model editing.
neurips-2022-locating-and-editing-factua.tldr: Causal interventions locate factual-recall computations in GPT, and ROME edits their weights to change specific factual associations.

paragraphs: Some machine-learning optimization problems choose an entire distribution or measure rather than a finite vector of parameters. This paper studies mirror descent in that infinite-dimensional setting. It defines Bregman divergences using directional derivatives and establishes convergence for pairs of functionals satisfying relative smoothness and convexity assumptions.

These assumptions allow the analysis to accommodate functionals such as Kullback–Leibler divergence even when ordinary smoothness is unavailable. Applied to joint distributions and KL divergence, the framework identifies the primal iterations of continuous entropic optimal transport’s Sinkhorn algorithm as mirror descent. This yields a new proof of its linear or sublinear convergence behavior.

The authors also show that expectation maximization can always formally be expressed as mirror descent. The convergence-rate result they state for EM concerns a more specific setting: optimizing the latent distribution while holding mixture parameters fixed. This setting corresponds to Richardson–Lucy deconvolution, for which they derive sublinear rates. The paper thus supplies a common optimization perspective while keeping the scope of its rate guarantees tied to the assumptions and particular problems analyzed.
neurips-2022-mirror-descent-with-relativ.tldr: The paper extends mirror-descent convergence analysis to measure spaces and applies it to Sinkhorn and a restricted EM setting.

paragraphs: A computation graph specifies dependencies between operations, but it can permit many valid execution orders. This paper learns to choose a topological order, focusing on minimizing memory use in compiler applications. The task combines a strict structural requirement—respecting the directed acyclic graph’s dependencies—with an optimization objective that distinguishes among valid orders.

The proposed encoder–decoder system uses Topoformer, an attention-based graph neural network. Its message passing incorporates different topological transformations of the input graph. The encoder produces representations for nodes, which become priorities. A decoder then uses those priorities to define a probability distribution over valid topological orders.

The authors train on synthetically generated layered graphs. On synthetic graphs with up to 2,000 nodes, their approach matches or improves on several ordering baselines while running significantly faster. They also train and evaluate it on real computation graphs, reporting performance improvements. These findings support learned ordering as a useful approach to compiler-related graph optimization, with the observed quality and speed advantages grounded in the evaluated graph collections rather than a guarantee of finding an optimal order.
neurips-2022-neural-topological-ordering.tldr: Topoformer learns node priorities for valid computation-graph orderings, improving or matching tested baselines with substantially faster synthetic-graph results.

paragraphs: Low-bit quantization can reduce Transformer memory and computation costs, but unusually large values make accurate quantization difficult. This paper investigates both the origin and importance of these outliers. The authors identify LayerNorm’s gamma parameter as an amplifier and find that some large values associated with a few tokens can be sharply clipped without harming performance.

Their framework combines Gamma Migration with Token-Wise Clipping. Gamma Migration moves the amplifying factor into subsequent modules through an equivalent transformation, producing a more quantization-friendly model without additional overhead. Token-Wise Clipping exploits differences in value ranges across tokens, using a coarse-to-fine procedure to select a clipping range that minimizes final quantization loss efficiently.

The method is designed for plug-and-play use. Extensive experiments show improvements over existing approaches, and the authors report that six-bit post-training quantization of BERT reaches full-precision performance in their evaluation. The significance lies in treating outliers according to their cause and contribution: preserving every extreme value is not always necessary for maintaining model quality, and restructuring the computation can make low-bit representations more effective.
neurips-2022-outlier-suppression-pushing.tldr: Gamma Migration and Token-Wise Clipping suppress quantization outliers, bringing six-bit post-training BERT to full-precision performance in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: A model can fit its training data perfectly and still predict well on new examples. This paper examines a separate consequence of having many parameters: vulnerability to membership inference. Such an attack tries to determine whether a particular example was used for training, so predictive generalization and protection of training membership are different concerns.

The authors prove that membership-inference vulnerability increases with parameter count for an overparameterized linear regression model with Gaussian data. This gives a theoretical foundation for a relationship previously studied largely through limited empirical evidence. Additional experiments indicate similar behavior in more complex nonlinear models, extending the empirical relevance without making the linear-model theorem universal.

The analysis also considers ridge-regularized linear regression. In the Gaussian-data setting and overparameterized regime, increasing regularization increases membership-inference vulnerability. This result is specifically tied to that setting rather than a claim about every form of regularization. Together, the findings reveal a privacy tradeoff that model accuracy alone does not capture: adding parameters, and even strengthening regularization in the analyzed regime, can make training membership easier to infer.
neurips-2022-parameters-or-privacy-a-pro.tldr: The paper proves that more parameters increase membership-inference vulnerability in Gaussian linear regression and finds similar empirical trends in nonlinear models.

paragraphs: Peer-prediction mechanisms reward reports when their truth cannot be checked directly. Traditional guarantees identify an equilibrium where everyone reports honestly, assuming Bayesian agents use fixed strategies across tasks. This paper asks what happens when participants instead learn and change their reporting behavior over a sequence of interactions.

The authors first show that no-regret learning alone does not guarantee convergence to truthful reporting. They then analyze a family of learning algorithms whose strategy updates depend only on cumulative rewards. For agents using algorithms in this family, they prove convergence to truthful reporting under the Correlated Agreement mechanism. The family includes multiplicative weight update and Follow the Perturbed Leader, but is not defined by the no-regret property.

Simulations show truthful convergence for several algorithms in the analyzed family and for epsilon-greedy, which falls outside it. The latter is empirical evidence rather than an extension of the theorem. The paper’s central contribution is to distinguish the existence of a truthful equilibrium from whether learning agents actually approach it, and to identify an algorithm family for which that dynamic behavior can be established.
neurips-2022-peer-prediction-for-learnin.tldr: No-regret learning alone cannot ensure honesty, but a specified reward-based learning family converges to truthful reporting under Correlated Agreement.

paragraphs: Domain generalization seeks models that work on unseen data distributions using experience from several training domains. This paper proposes a probabilistic objective between average performance and worst-case protection. Its key modeling assumption is that training and test domains are draws from a shared underlying distribution over domains, allowing observed shifts to inform which future shifts are probable.

Quantile Risk Minimization targets a chosen quantile of the predictor’s risk across domains. Choosing probability level alpha asks for a predictor whose risk is low with probability alpha under that domain distribution. This makes the desired coverage explicit, rather than treating all possible shifts as equally relevant or summarizing them only through their average.

The authors introduce Empirical QRM as a practical algorithm and establish a generalization bound. They also identify conditions under which it recovers the causal predictor as alpha approaches one; that recovery is conditional. A quantile-focused evaluation protocol accompanies experiments on WILDS and DomainBed datasets, where EQRM outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The results support evaluating robustness through the distribution of domain-level outcomes, as well as optimizing for it.
neurips-2022-probable-domain-generalizat.tldr: Quantile Risk Minimization targets strong performance with a chosen probability over domains drawn from a shared meta-distribution.

paragraphs: Test-time training adapts a deployed model to shifted target data when the full source dataset is unavailable and predictions are needed immediately. This paper argues that inconsistent experimental assumptions have made comparisons between methods unfair. It revisits those assumptions, categorizes protocols using two key factors, and adopts a sequential protocol intended to reflect realistic deployment.

Within that setting, the authors develop test-time anchored clustering, or TTAC. The approach identifies clusters in source and target domains and matches target clusters to source clusters to improve feature learning and generalization. Pseudo-label filtering and iterative updates are added to make the clustering procedure more effective and efficient.

Across six test-time-training datasets, TTAC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods under all protocols evaluated in the paper. The contribution has two parts: a method for adapting representations through cluster matching, and a clearer basis for evaluating adaptation methods. The protocol analysis matters because a performance comparison is meaningful only in light of the information access and inference conditions available to each method, making comparisons within the same protocol central to the authors’ recommendation.
neurips-2022-revisiting-realistic-test-t.tldr: TTAC adapts models through source–target cluster matching while the paper clarifies protocols for fair test-time-training comparisons.

paragraphs: S-PIFu reconstructs a clothed human from a single image by incorporating a parametric body model into a pixel-aligned implicit reconstruction model. Its contribution is three ways to communicate information from that body model to the reconstruction process. These additions supply image-aligned features, structural labels, and body-part orientation information.

First, ray-based sampling transforms the parametric model into informative two-dimensional feature maps aligned with image pixels. Second, features derived from blendweights provide soft labels for human body parts. These labels help improve the structural fidelity of the resulting mesh. The two strategies make body-model information usable both through alignment with the image and through guidance about body structure.

Third, the method extracts body-part orientations from the parametric model and uses them to improve reconstruction quality further. Together, the three strategies form the S-PIFu framework. The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on every metric in their evaluation. The stated result supports combining these complementary forms of body information: the framework uses the parametric model through several specific representations that contribute to reconstruction rather than through a single undifferentiated input.
neurips-2022-s-pifu-integrating-parametr.tldr: S-PIFu improves single-image clothed-human reconstruction using ray-based features, blendweight labels, and body-part orientations from a parametric model.

paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent lets workers compute updates at their own pace and send them to a server without waiting for one another. Some updates therefore arrive late. For smooth non-convex objectives, earlier convergence guarantees depended on the longest delay, potentially making one unusually slow update dominate the theoretical assessment.

The paper sharpens that analysis without changing the algorithm. In the delay-dependent part of the iteration bound, it replaces maximum delay with the geometric mean of maximum and average delay. This can substantially improve the guarantee when average delay is much smaller. A second contribution adapts the learning rate to delay, reducing that dependence to average delay alone without extra communication or additional hyperparameter tuning.

These bounds concern reaching an approximate stationary point, with the stochastic-gradient variance term retained. Within the paper’s analysis, they establish that asynchronous SGD is always faster than mini-batch SGD. The authors also study heterogeneous worker objectives motivated by federated learning, proving a weaker dependence on maximum delay than earlier work. The central advance is showing how typical delays, rather than only the worst delay, can govern stronger performance guarantees.
neurips-2022-sharper-convergence-guarant.tldr: Sharper asynchronous-SGD bounds replace worst-delay dependence with average-delay-sensitive terms, with further gains from delay-adaptive learning rates.

paragraphs: ShuffleMixer aims to reconstruct higher-resolution images with a lightweight convolutional network suitable for mobile-oriented design. The paper explores large convolution kernels and channel splitting and shuffling as a way to mix image features efficiently. Its basic component combines a large depth-wise convolution with two projection layers built around those channel operations.

The design also addresses a limitation of relying on large depth-wise convolutions alone: they are insufficient for reconstructing fine details in locally correlated natural images. The authors add Fused-MBConv components to model local connections between different features while maintaining the module’s efficiency. The architecture therefore combines broad spatial processing with additional local feature interaction.

Experiments show competitive super-resolution performance while using about one-third the parameters and floating-point operations of efficient state-of-the-art methods such as CARN. Those reductions describe model size and operation counts, rather than a measured universal device speedup. The findings support the paper’s architectural argument that large kernels can fit an efficient super-resolution design when channel mixing and local connectivity are handled carefully.
neurips-2022-shufflemixer-an-efficient-c.tldr: ShuffleMixer combines large depth-wise convolutions and channel mixing to deliver competitive super-resolution with substantially fewer parameters and operations.

paragraphs: Submodular maximization selects items under diminishing returns: adding an item contributes less as the selected set grows. This paper studies monotone objectives under resource constraints. It gives a deterministic algorithm that achieves at least half the optimal value under a knapsack constraint while using a number of function queries linear in the number of candidate items.

The result also enables a deterministic linear-time algorithm attaining the tight one-minus-one-over-e approximation under a size constraint. Complementary lower bounds explain why much smaller query budgets can be inadequate. When the allowed selection size is constant, sublinear function evaluations cannot guarantee any constant approximation, whether the algorithm is deterministic or randomized.

When the selection size is a constant fraction of all items, the authors establish a further threshold: below order n divided by log n evaluations, an algorithm cannot outperform a uniformly random subset of the required size. They extend their results to combinations of a p-set system and multiple knapsack constraints. Evaluations cover recommendation and several summarization applications, connecting the theoretical guarantees and query limits to practical selection problems.
neurips-2022-submodular-maximization-in-.tldr: The paper gives deterministic linear-query submodular maximization guarantees and lower bounds showing when fewer evaluations cannot suffice.

paragraphs: This paper uses pretrained vision and language models to produce detailed image descriptions without additional cross-modal training. Its central idea is to let the models communicate through structured text. A vision model first extracts semantic information from an image, including tags, object attributes, locations, and captions, and organizes it into a prompt called visual clues.

The language model uses those clues to generate several comprehensive descriptions of the image. The vision model then checks the candidates and selects the one that best aligns with the visual content. Vision therefore plays two roles: supplying information before generation and assessing image alignment afterward. The language model provides the descriptive expansion between those stages.

Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of the structured semantic representation. The approach matters because it connects the zero-shot capabilities of existing foundation models through an explicit interface, without requiring another round of training to link the modalities. The findings support the usefulness of visual clues for paragraph captioning, while the verification step gives candidate selection a direct connection back to the image.
neurips-2022-visual-clues-bridging-visio.tldr: Structured visual clues connect pretrained vision and language models to generate and select image paragraphs without extra cross-modal training.
